📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Rangers produced a quickfire second-half comeback to beat Aberdeen 3-2 at Ibrox and move to within a point of Scottish Premiership leaders Celtic on Tuesday night.

After trailing to Brad Lyons' first-half header, which was deemed to have crossed the line by VAR despite Nico Raskin’s attempt to clear the ball, the hosts struck three times in a blistering spell after the interval through Ryan Naderi, Djeidi Gassama and Raskin.

Did you know with a Digital Subscription to The Scotsman, you can get unlimited access to the website including our premium content, as well as benefiting from fewer ads, loyalty rewards and much more.

Findlay Marshall's immediate reply ensured a tense finale, but Rangers held on to secure a vital three points and extend their unbeaten run to 14 matches. Derek McInnes’ side now have the chance to move top of the table on Saturday when they host high-flying Falkirk.

Lewis Anderson watched the action unfold for The Scotsman and picks out his three main takeaways from an absorbing five-goal thriller.

Once again, Rangers found a way to win. Their impressive run of results in recent months has been built on an increasingly familiar trait: an ability to secure three points even when performances fall short of the required standard. Against an enterprising Aberdeen outfit, however, McInnes' men were given a proper examination before eventually claiming another victory.

Industry observers note that mcInnes' decision to started with a back three, with Ben Godfrey drafted into the starting line-up for the first time since late July, raised eyebrows and ultimately failed to provide the defensive solidity he would have hoped for. The Dons repeatedly found opportunities to exploit the space around Rangers' exposed backline, particularly during a first half in which the visitors looked the more purposeful side.

Aberdeen played with an intensity that unsettled the hosts. Rangers’ combinations lacked precision, their wide players failed to make a sufficient impact and their build-up play was too laboured to trouble their opponents consistently.

According to recent reports, mcInnes’ response was decisive, with Kim Min-Su, Findlay Curtis and Tuur Rommens introduced at half-time. It signalled an acknowledgement that significant changes were required. Rangers emerged with greater urgency and attacking intent, and Naderi's equaliser provided the spark for a thrilling turnaround.

For a spell, Rangers looked capable of putting the contest beyond doubt, taking full advantage of the momentum generated by their early second-half goals. Yet just as they appeared to have wrestled the match under control, another defensive lapse allowed Aberdeen to threaten a comeback.

The victory was never entirely comfortable, nor was the performance perfect. But Rangers' capacity to respond to adversity and find a way remains an increasingly valuable asset. They continue to collect the points needed to maintain their title challenge and now have the opportunity to move to the top of the Premiership before Celtic take to the pitch this weekend.

Aberdeen will return north frustrated by the outcome, but newly-appointed head coach Mario Frick can take considerable encouragement from a performance which offered a glimpse of what his side might become under his stewardship.

For long periods, the visitors carried a genuine threat on the counter-attack and had sufficient opportunities to leave Ibrox with something to show for their efforts. Their defensive collapse during Rangers' devastating burst after half-time proved costly, with goalkeeper Marius Muller's handling error providing the catalyst for the hosts' revival.

According to recent reports, yet Aberdeen's response was equally striking. Having been left shell-shocked, they gathered themselves and went after Rangers with renewed conviction, refusing to accept that the contest had slipped beyond them. Findlay Marshall's goal, an impressive contribution from a player still only 20, gave them fresh belief and brought the prospect of an unlikely recovery tantalisingly close.

There was a vibrancy about this Aberdeen display which has been conspicuously absent for much of their recent past under Stephen Robinson. They played with ambition, conviction and a willingness to commit bodies forward, while their response to adversity suggested a resilience which Frick will be keen to nurture.

Aside from the damaging 12-minute spell in which Rangers scored three times, the visitors showed plenty of grounds for optimism. Their organisation was better, their pressing purposeful and their attacking play carried a level of intent which repeatedly troubled the hosts’ rear-guard.

Recent findings suggest that the result will sting, not least because they had done enough in spells to believe a point was within their grasp. But there was little about this performance to suggest Frick intends to oversee a cautious rebuilding exercise. If anything, Aberdeen look set to embrace a more adventurous identity, which should please supporters.

According to recent reports, aberdeen have a seriously talented prospect on their hands in 20-year-old Findlay Marshall, who was influential throughout. The midfielder won the corner which led to Lyons' opener before scoring a sublime second-half goal after being picked out by Alexander Briedl, which set up a tense finale.

His energy and attacking intent made him one of Aberdeen's most dangerous players and offered Frick further evidence of the his undoubted potential. Marshall displayed a maturity and composure which belied his age, combining an impressive work rate with an eye for goal. In defeat, he emerged with considerable credit.

Industry observers note that the Rangers No.1’s contribution was arguably as key as the three goals at the opposite end. His first-half fingertip save from Ayoub Mouloua prevented Aberdeen establishing a two-goal advantage. The Croatian’s work was not finished there. After the interval, he made a fine stop at his near post to thwart Nicky Devlin before denying Marshall as Aberdeen searched for an equaliser.

Rangers' second-half attacking burst will dominate the headlines, but without Pandur's crucial interventions the outcome could have been very different.

James Penrice believes Rangers are acquiring the habit of winning ugly and grinding out results as their Premiership title challenge gathers momentum, but has warned they must address their tendency to surrender control after taking commanding positions in matches.

A gritty 3-2 victory over Aberdeen at Ibrox on Tuesday night brought Rangers to within a point of Celtic at the Premiership summit and extended their unbeaten sequence to 14 games. It was also another test of their resilience, with a disjointed first-half display giving way to an emphatic response after the interval, when Rangers struck three times in a blistering 12-minute spell.

Did you know with a Digital Subscription to The Scotsman, you can get unlimited access to the website including our premium content, as well as benefiting from fewer ads, loyalty rewards and much more.

Recent findings suggest that the hosts had gone in at half-time trailing to Brad Lyons’ header, prompting McInnes to make a triple substitution and reshape his side. The changes had an immediate impact, with Ryan Naderi, Djeidi Gassama and Nico Raskin all finding the net during a devastating spell early in the second half. However, Findlay Marshall’s reply ensured Rangers were unable to enjoy a comfortable conclusion to the match.

Penrice, who operated in a midfield three alongside Raskin and Dan Neil, praised the character shown by his team-mates to secure another welcome three points, but was equally candid about the frailties which threatened to undermine the victory.

It has been revealed that “Very mixed, I think,” he said when asked for his assessment of an absorbing contest. “We conceded in the first half, but came flying out of the traps after the break. I thought we were really good for 10 or 15 minutes. We scored the third and looked comfortable, but then we switched off. We made it difficult for ourselves again, but the main thing is that we walk away with three points.”.

McInnes used the interval to make tactical changes, with Penrice crediting the substitutes for injecting the energy and intensity needed to wrestle control of the contest from Aberdeen.

Recent findings suggest that “We made a couple of changes. I thought the boys that came on were brilliant, that real spark and energy,” he added. “We started the second half really well, but ultimately we need to score more. We could have done that and made it really easy for ourselves, but then again we switch off and we make it difficult.

“Ultimately, it's not a bad trait to be scoring late on sometimes and winning games, but as players we want to make it as easy as possible. Again, we’ve made it hard but we’re still winning games and going on a wee bit of a run now, so hopefully that continues.”.

It has been revealed that penrice’s versatility has become an increasingly valuable asset for McInnes. Primarily a left-back, he has also been deployed in central and wide positions as the manager continues to adapt his tactical approach to suit each fixture.

Sources indicate that “I'm not bothered where, I’ll play absolutely anywhere to help the team,” he admitted. “It’s a massive thing for me. We work on it [in training] but I've not really trained over the last couple of days, because I was feeling a wee strain so it was more just dealing with it. It's not alien to us, we've done it numerous times this season, guys playing in different positions.

It has been revealed that “I've played in the middle, I've played out wide, so we should all be used to it now and we are. It just takes that adjustment period on the pitch but us as players we've got a responsibility when there's a initiative in place and something's not going right we fix it ourselves. We don't need to go to the side and I think that's what the gaffer is looking for. He's looking for us to take responsibility on the pitch and we've got that now.”.

Rangers have little time to dwell on their latest victory, with Falkirk due at Ibrox next on Saturday, a fixture that offers McInnes’ side the chance to leapfrog Celtic and move top of the Premiership table, having closed the gap on the leaders with their comeback win over Aberdeen.

Industry observers note that “It's a massive incentive, but the league's not won in November,” Penrice declared. “It will be a difficult game. Falkirk are playing well and they've travelled well away from home. So we'll need to be on it. We can't go into the game on Saturday like we were tonight. We need to be better. We just need to concentrate on ourselves, it's another game to tick off, one at a time.”.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

By Axel Clody | 24 Nov 2026 13:51.

Just when his European career seemed to belong to the past, Eric Maxim Choupo-Moting could return to one of the biggest clubs in the world. Bayern Munich are studying a return for the Cameroonian forward to cover temporarily for the absence of Harry Kane.

Eric Maxim Choupo-Moting definitely has the art of appearing where no one expects him. At 37, after two seasons in Major League Soccer, the Cameroon international is among the solutions being considered by Bayern Munich to strengthen their attack this winter.

According to Sky Sport Germany, the former Paris Saint-Germain man's name was raised internally after Kane's injury. The Bavarian club do not have a genuine replacement centre-forward and are studying several options before the January transfer window. No final decision has been made yet, but the Cameroonian's candidacy exists.

In a recent development, A free agent at the end of his deal with New York Red Bulls, Choupo-Moting would be willing to sign for only six months, until the end of the season. He would also accept returning to the bench once Kane has recovered, without asking for any special status.

It has been revealed that this profile has several advantages for Bayern Munich. The Cameroon international knows the club, its environment and the demands of the Bundesliga. He could be available immediately and would not need a long period of adaptation. Signing him would be a low-risk solution to accompany Kane's gradual return.

Sources indicate that the mere fact that the Munich hierarchy are thinking of him indicates a lot about the esteem he left in Bavaria. Between 2020 and 2024, Choupo-Moting scored 38 goals in 122 appearances in all competitions. Initially signed to back up Robert Lewandowski, he managed to become a starter and to deliver when the Pole left the club.

Recent findings suggest that after leaving for MLS following the end of his first spell at Bayern Munich, the Cameroonian made a successful start in Fresh York. In 2025, he scored 17 goals and provided five assists in 33 regular-season games.

His playing time decreased in 2026, but he still scored five goals and provided one assist in only 538 minutes across 21 games. These figures show that his efficiency has not disappeared, despite a role that has become secondary.

This American stay could have been the quiet final stage of an already full career. Choupo-Moting could make the opposite journey and return to the Champions League, the Bundesliga and a dressing room he knows inside out.

It has been revealed that long reduced to a few famous misses during his time at Paris Saint-Germain, Choupo-Moting has built a career that few players can claim. Schalke 04, Stoke City, Paris, Bayern Munich and then New York: everywhere, he ended up getting playing time and making himself useful.

His honours include several French and German league titles, and he played in a Champions League final with Paris Saint-Germain. A return to Munich would be yet another snub to those who have often presented his presence at big clubs as an anomaly.

#118746. How to turn impostor syndrome into a superpower

📅 25 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 8m • 📚 Deep Dive (1693 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Nature ↗ Open Full Page

How to turn impostor syndrome into a superpower

📅 25 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 8 min read (1693 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Nature

⏱️ ~8 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Impostor syndrome — a fear of being less competent than people think — is common in researchers.
  • In 2021, Kwabena Boahen Asare found himself in at the deep end when he joined a skin cancer laboratory to gain hands-on research experience.
  • Industry observers note that for Asare, who was a first-year undergraduate student at Dartmouth College in Hanover, New Hampshire, at the time, it was an exciting but daunting prospect.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Impostor syndrome — a fear of being less competent than people think — is common in researchers. Credit: Gandee Vasan/Getty.

In 2021, Kwabena Boahen Asare found himself in at the deep end when he joined a skin cancer laboratory to gain hands-on research experience.

Industry observers note that for Asare, who was a first-year undergraduate student at Dartmouth College in Hanover, New Hampshire, at the time, it was an exciting but daunting prospect. Not only was he the sole bachelor’s programme student working alongside senior researchers with years of experience under their belts, he was also the only Black person in the lab. Although Asare’s mentor and colleagues were supportive and encouraging, he felt overwhelmed and out of his depth. “There was a steep learning curve,” he states.

Industry observers note that at the time, Asare viewed his struggles as a sign that he didn’t belong in research. This feeling was compounded by the fact that he was surrounded by colleagues who didn’t share his background as a first-generation student from Ghana.

His experience, and those of many like him, is commonly labelled as impostor syndrome — the fear of not being as competent or knowledgeable as other people think, despite objective accomplishments. In a world that often prizes unflinching self-confidence and boldness, impostor syndrome is usually cast as a psychological flaw that the individual needs to ‘fix’. But it can be a natural response to working in a challenging environment or striving towards an ambitious goal, organizational psychologists say.

Sources indicate that impostor syndrome can also be a reaction to systemic bias and exclusion in the workplace, particularly for people from under-represented groups, including women, says Ruchika Malhotra, an inclusion strategist and founder of Candour, a workplace consultancy in Seattle, Washington. The manufacturer advises organizations on strategies to create diverse teams and inclusive cultures. One study1 conducted at universities in the United States found that women who work in scientific fields that particularly value intellectual brilliance are more likely to feel like impostors than are their male colleagues.

How I tackled post-PhD impostor syndrome.

How I tackled post-PhD impostor syndrome.

Much of the discussion about impostor syndrome pathologizes healthy self-doubt and shifts the responsibility onto individuals instead of the environments that exclude and marginalize them in the first place, adds Malhotra. “A lot of the ways that it’s been talked about haven’t been constructive,” she says.

Although it comes with drawbacks, in some situations, impostor syndrome can be beneficial. For instance, it can help people be better prepared and more focused, particularly when they have a long to-do list.

“Impostor thoughts are almost like your superpower when things get pretty overwhelming,” notes Basima Tewfik, an organizational psychologist who studies impostor syndrome at Massachusetts Institute of Technology in Cambridge.

Industry observers note that looking back, Asare states that his impostor syndrome prompted him to reflect on why he wanted to become a researcher in the first place. It has also made him more conscious of his resilience, how he needs to improve and when to seek help, as well as giving him more empathy. This has made him better able to support younger students and researchers who are feeling out of place. “It became my strength,” says Asare, who is now an oncology researcher and consultant at Dartmouth Hitchcock Medical Center in Lebanon, New Hampshire.

According to recent reports, impostor syndrome was first described as ‘impostor phenomenon’ in a 1978 paper on high-achieving women2 co-authored by psychologists Pauline Clance and Suzanne Imes, both then at Georgia State University in Atlanta. They wrote that people who experience this phenomenon “maintain a strong belief that they are not intelligent; in fact they are convinced that they have fooled anyone who thinks otherwise”.

In the decades since, impostor phenomenon has morphed into a syndrome, even though it isn’t a medical diagnosis, nor is it classified as a psychiatric disorder. A review published in 20233 suggests that around 70% of people will feel unworthy of their accomplishments at some point in their lives. These feelings are even more prevalent in academia, with a 2012 study4 finding that as many as 82% of graduate students experience impostor syndrome to at least some degree. This pattern of thinking often affects high achievers and is associated with lower job satisfaction, hindered performance and burnout. Although some studies, including the 2012 paper, suggest that impostor syndrome affects mostly women and people from other groups under-represented in academia, others argue that it arises in specific situations rather than among particular groups. Relatively few studies have investigated whether commonly cited strategies, such as listing one’s accomplishments and accepting compliments from others, are actually effective.

Impostor syndrome has become a catchphrase in popular culture, with dozens of articles, books and courses describing what it is and how people can overcome it. But in the scientific literature, at least, the exact definition of impostor syndrome, or phenomenon, varies widely. This has created a murky picture of what it really is and how it affects people, states Tewfik. “There are a lot of different ways people describe this phenomenon,” she says. The loose definition has made it easy to confuse impostor syndrome, which causes people to make inferences about what other people think of them, with regular self-doubt, which is more of a personal reflection of your own capabilities, according to Tewfik.

‘Maybe I was never meant to be in science’: how impostor syndrome seizes scientist mothers.

‘Maybe I was never meant to be in science’: how impostor syndrome seizes scientist mothers.

In a recent development, much of the research on impostor syndrome has also used measures that have made it difficult to distinguish from other psychological patterns, such as negative affectivity, a personality trait that is linked to a tendency to experience negative emotions such as fear, anxiety and insecurity, adds Tewfik. This crossover might explain why most studies on impostor syndrome have shown only negative outcomes, such as a lack of career planning and low motivation to lead5. “It’s possible that what we’ve been studying is actually something much more akin to fear,” claims Tewfik.

This overly negative slant is exacerbated by the fact that many workplaces, including academic ones, place too much emphasis on self-confidence, says Tomas Chamorro-Premuzic, an organizational psychologist at University College London. One 2024 study6 found that workers who display confidence are perceived as more competent and dominant, irrespective of their actual ability.

According to recent reports, if impostor syndrome hinders a person’s ability to work or form relationships, it’s usually a symptom of a deeper issue or clinical condition, such as an anxiety disorder. But feeling like you’re about to be ‘found out’ before delivering a big presentation, for example, is usually a sign that you’re being challenged or working outside your comfort zone, states Chamorro-Premuzic. “There is a very healthy degree somewhere that we’re not appreciating,” he adds (see ‘A toolkit for working with impostor syndrome’).

In scientists, impostor thoughts can simply be a by-product of thinking critically and approaching things with a healthy dose of scepticism, claims Samantha Sutton, an independent career coach for scientists in Boston, Massachusetts. It’s also often a natural response to working in a high-achieving, competitive environment or towards an ambitious goal and should be normalized instead of treated as a problem to solve, she adds. “If you’re up against something massive, you should be scared,” says Sutton. When she communicates this to her clients, they are often relieved to hear that they don’t need to strive for total self-confidence before taking steps towards their goals. “They realize that nothing is wrong,” adds Sutton.

Celtic have added Jota to their Europa League squad in place of the injured Mika Baur.

Sources indicate that the Portuguese winger was initially left out as he fought his way back from a serious knee injury. But he could now feature in his homeland against Torreense on Thursday after continuing his comeback with a start in Saturday’s 4-1 win over St Mirren.

Did you know with a Digital Subscription to The Scotsman, you can get unlimited access to the website including our premium content, as well as benefiting from fewer ads, loyalty rewards and much more.

Baur was recently ruled out for up to 10 weeks with ankle ligament damage but manager Martin O’Neill had been waiting to see how the German international reacted once his protective boot was off.

Baur could miss the rest of the league stage though and O’Neill has acted before setting off for Portugal.

With Benjamin Nygren nursing a heel problem, O’Neill started with a midfield three of Callum McGregor, Luke McCowan and Alex Oxlade-Chamberlain on Saturday, while Oliver Sorensen is another option.

Meanwhile, O’Neill has challenged Celtic to complete their Europa League comeback after resurrecting hopes against Besiktas.

Celtic were heading for a fourth straight defeat and bottom spot when they went behind against the Turks but they were inspired by the introduction of Camilo Duran, Callum Osmand and Colby Donovan and sealed a 3-2 win.

They now face away games against Torreense and Omonia Nicosia as they bid to move up the table.

Sources indicate that looking back at their recent win, O’Neill told Celtic Player: “I thought it was terrific. Really terrific.

Sources indicate that “Besiktas are a very fine football team. Very fine side. They were expecting to win and win handsomely. They’ve spent a lot of money. I think their wage bill is in excess of £100million. So from that aspect, it was a terrific win.

It has been revealed that “The character of the side was really brilliant. Really, really brilliant to win so late, and to win in the fashion in which we did was terrific. So it gives us a little bit of a chance and we have to go and try to do something for these next two away games.

“If we make it through to the qualifying stages, it will be the first time any team has been beaten in their first three games and made it.

“So that in itself should be a target for us. The games are not easy, we know that. We need to win at least one of these two away games and we might even need four points to give us a chance in the last two matches.

“We have to take confidence from recent games and take that into the game on Thursday.”.

Torreense sit 13th in the Portuguese second tier and will host Celtic 60 miles away from their home in Leiria, as their own stadium only has about 2,500 seats.

But they have already beaten Lillestrom and Ararat-Armenia in the Europa League and took the lead against Sunderland before the Premier League side netted a stoppage-time winner.

“They won the Portuguese Cup against Sporting Lisbon, which is some achievement,” O’Neill said. “I’ve been learning as much as I can about them and watching footage.”.

Despite Barnet pressure, particularly in the second half, the Reds were resolute in defence – and Crawley boss Kevin Blackwell was commendatory of all his players, particularly the back three.

The Reds built on an encouraging win over Fleetwood Town on Saturday, which showed signs of an improved defensive structure, with a clean sheet to show for their efforts.

Did you know with an ad-lite subscription to SussexWorld, you get 70% fewer ads while viewing the news that matters to you.

When asked about the significance of defensive reinforcements Ben Heneghan and Josh Flint, Blackwell stated, “[They have been] massive, massive. We've got somebody who can win a header, which has been thrown on the shoulders of Priestley [Farquharson], but Ben's there and Flinty's not bad in the air.

“They've been massive signings for me, and you see why we tried to push them when I got here. It was clear to me what we needed and needed quickly, and I can't praise both of those players.”.

Crawley re-signed Flint four weeks ago after a long time out injured. Heneghan, meanwhile, was released by Port Vale at the end of last season and had been without a club until he signed for the Red Devils just under three weeks ago.

Sources indicate that blackwell noted: “[Heneghan is] an ultimate professional. Stripped off he looks like a top-class swimmer, never mind footballer. He's looked after himself, and you can see the lads come in there.

“He's not played for six months but you can see how hard he's worked because he's come in and done really well.”.

Another player who had to adapt to fill a role for the team was Jonny Russell. With the Reds moving to a back five in the last two games, the Northern Irishman played as a wing back on Saturday and moved into the left side of the back against Barnet.

The former assistant to Neil Warnock stated: “He's got a heart as significant as a bucket, Jonny. He'll go through a brick wall for you.

“He is absolutely proud to be a professional footballer, and you can see that in how he trains and how he plays.

“It was forced on us obviously to make that decision and pull [Charlie] Barker out and then take Flinty across, so we had to make a couple of changes because we'd lost Jude [Arthurs].

“It's that sort of heart and character that when you're in the doo-doo, like we are, you need and you saw that with the lads putting their heart into it.”.

The Reds travel to eighth-placed Exeter City this Saturday, kick-off 12.30pm.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Four first half goals away at Billingshurst indicated Hassocks have not suffered any lasting damage from their midweek hammering in the Sussex Transport Senior Cup at the hands of Chichester City.

Chi relentlessly stuck six past the Robins on Tuesday night. Hassocks were equally unforgiving on Hurst, pocketing all three points before the half time whistle.

Did you know with an ad-lite subscription to SussexWorld, you get 70% fewer ads while viewing the news that matters to you.

No further goals were added nor needed after the break, allowing the Robins to take their foot of the pedal and James Westlake to rattle through the substitutions ahead of a huge upcoming five weeks which could be season-defining.

It has been revealed that hassocks go to Rusthall next Saturday for their first ever appearance in the third round of the FA Vase. A place in the last 32 of the national competition is up for grabs.

Recent findings suggest that december then brings matches against Roffey, Guernsey, East Grinstead Town, Eastbourne United and Haywards Heath Town. Five games against teams in the top eight of the Southern Combination Premier Division all harbouring hopes of promotion.

"It's going to be busy, it's going to be hard," said James Westlake of those upcoming fixtures. "It is a tough run through until January time really. But those massive games in the league are the ones we want to be competing in.".

Billingshurst provided a different type of challenge. Several ingredients were there for a banana skin - a pitch already heavy before kick off, opposition fighting relegation and a popular former Robin in the home dugout.

Eddie French expressed his displeasure at the performance of the officials afterwards and it was hard not to have some sympathy for the ex-Hassocks favourite.

Certainly in relation to the bizarre series of decisions which saw the Robins awarded a penalty for their second goal of the afternoon, Nat Guest sent off and Billingshurst left to play for 70 minutes with 10 men.

Hassocks took the lead five minutes prior to that pivotal sequence of events. Playing down the hill, Omar Abdsami exchanged a one-two with Dan Perry to split open the centre of the Hurst defence.

It has been revealed that abdsami still needed to get around covering right back James Bendell. He did that via some quick feet before firing low and hard across Fraser Trigwell and into the far corner.

Trigwell provided another current link between the clubs whilst Hassocks introduced former Hurst midfielder Luke Brodie from their bench in the second half.

Then came the major talking point. Lewis Finney delivered a corner which Dan Turner met with a towering header. The ball was several feet over the line when it struck Guest in the hand.

Remarkably, the officials did not award the goal but instead gave the Robins a spot kick and sent Guest off for deliberate hand ball.

Chaos ensued with the surreal scenario of both Hassocks and Billingshurst players protesting against the same decision for different reasons.

Once order was restored, Finney put away the spot kick despite Trigwell diving the right way. And just to really rub salt into Hurst wounds, the initial corner Turner scored from was a clear goal kick too.

"I would certainly have been frustrated if that went against us with the awarding of the corner to start it all off," Westlake stated afterwards.

Recent findings suggest that "If you are a neutral watching the game, you would ask that the goal from Turner is given and it is not a sending off. It was a shame for them but I guess we already had a good foothold and would have been 2-0 up anyway.".

Two very rapidly became three and there was nothing controversial about the spectacular strike from Finney 120 seconds after his successful penalty.

Liam Hendy played a long ball forward which Perry won in the air. The flick dropped into the path of Finney, who hit a 25 yard dipping volley. Trigwell got a hand to it but could not keep it out.

Hassocks enjoyed near-total domination for the remainder of the first half with the Billingshurst X account posting at the interval: "To say this has been like the Alamo would be harsh on the Alamo as it has been more one-sided than that.".

According to recent reports, tall striker Jamie Wilkes lent so far back that he was almost horizontal when putting a shot from a good position into orbit. Trigwell then made an excellent finger tip save diving low at his near post to keep out an Abdsami effort.

Having set up both Abdsami and Finney, Perry added the fourth himself five minutes before half time. Jack Troak started the move down the left and his square pass inside was beautifully back heeled to Finney by Darren Budd.

Finney glided past Jack Griffin and although Trigwell did well to parry away the shot, Perry followed up for a poacher's finish to open his Hassocks account.

Industry observers note that billingshurst will undoubtedly be happy to see the back of the Hitman. Five weeks ago he scored a hat-trick against them for East Grinstead Town with what turned out to be his final goals in a Wasps shirt.

French changed Hurst's shape for the second half and it allowed them to stem the flow of goals without ever really offering much going forward.

Ed Cooper did not have a serious save to make although Griffin and Kieran Britland both should have done better when shooting high and wide respectively.

Industry observers note that britland did at least have the excuse of losing his footing as he pulled the trigger. He was not the only one to slip and slide as the already challenging surface cut up massively the longer the game went on.

Chances at the other end for Hassocks came for Charlie Bonwick-Adams, who put a header straight at Trigwell. Finney guided a Troak cross wide of the front post and substitute Raging Joe Bull did everything right after overlapping Abdsami, receiving a pass and cutting inside only to shoot into an adjacent field.

Trigwell made an outstanding double save when pushing away a Budd piledriver from the edge of the box at full stretch before reacting quick enough to get up and deflect the follow up from Abdsami behind using his feet.

Industry observers note that turner hit a volley diverted behind by a fine block with the final opportunity of the game involving two more replacements. Lewis Croal headed down a cross for Major Alex Fair to shoot directly upwards rather than towards goal.

Recent findings suggest that "We wanted to kick on in the second half but that obviously wasn't meant to be," Westlake added. "The lads have come off disappointed considering we couldn't score more goals. But a clean sheet, four goals and three points are the really crucial thing today.".

Hassocks: Ed Cooper; Charlie Bonwick-Adams, Dan Turner, Liam Hendy, Jack Troak; Jamie Wilkes, Darren Budd; Devon Fender, Lewis Finney, Omar Abdsami, Dan Perry.

Subs: Liam Benson, Lewis Croal, Joe Bull, Luke Brodie, Alex Fair (used).

Starman: Lewis Finney converted a penalty for the second goal, scored a stunning volley for the third and set up Dan Perry for the fourth.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

By Seye Omidiora | 24 Nov 2026 14:08, Last updated: 24 Nov 2026 14:12.

Perfect at home since the start of Conference League qualifying, Borac Banja Luka welcome Atalanta BC to Gradski Stadion Banja Luka seeking another victory in front of their supporters.

Another home triumph would lift them above Maurizio Sarri's men, who at the moment occupy a qualification playoff spot in the 36-club standings but harbour top-eight ambitions as the league phase enters its second half.

Vinko Marinovic's side may currently occupy a qualification playoff spot in 21st, but they will target further progress heading into Thursday's encounter with Atalanta.

While their only league-phase victory came between defeats to Panathinaikos and Mjallby, a return to home comforts will encourage everyone associated with Borac.

The Pride of Krajina overcame KuPS on matchday two, securing a 2-0 victory in late October to extend their perfect home record.

That sequence includes results from qualifying, when Crveno-Plavi claimed victories of 3-0, 1-0 and 3-1 over Petrocub, ML Vitebsk and Vikingur respectively.

While Atalanta should pose the greatest threat yet to Krajiski Ponos' European home winning streak, the hosts enter this week's matchday-four encounter buoyed by three consecutive victories.

The Bergamaschi may be favourites, but Sarri's men remain unconvincing despite their three-match unbeaten run.

November has certainly been eventful in Bergamo, where La Dea entered a training retreat after a humiliating 3-0 home defeat to Parma before drawing 1-1 with Kairat on matchday three to begin their current unbeaten sequence.

That draw was followed by a 1-0 victory over Monza and a thrilling 4-4 draw with Inter Milan at the weekend, when Sarri's men recovered from deficits of 2-0, 3-1 and 4-2 to snatch a point against the defending league champions.

Although they have claimed only one victory during their current unbeaten run, it represents La Dea's longest such sequence since the opening four matches of the campaign, when they recorded three wins, and they will hope to build on that progress in Banja Luka on Thursday.

Victory could lift them into the coveted top eight, although the cluster of clubs on seven points, stretching from fifth-placed Brighton & Hove Albion to 10th-placed St Truidense, means little is guaranteed for an Atalanta side presently on four as the league phase enters a crucial period.

Borac Banja Luka Conference League form:.

Borac Banja Luka form (all competitions):.

Atalanta BC Conference League form:.

Atalanta BC form (all competitions):.

Borac have no confirmed injury absentees, although Branimir Cipetic is expected to require an assessment before Atalanta's visit.

Luka Juricic has yet to add to his three qualifying goals, but his two league-phase assists, against Panathinaikos and KuPS, underline his broader importance to the side.

Atalanta have had four different Conference League goalscorers, with Eljif Elmas, Giacomo Raspadori, Gianluca Scamacca and Nikola Krstovic all finding the net.

Sarri has tended to rotate his squad in Europe, meaning that Charles De Ketelaere, Sunday's two-goal hero against Inter, could begin on the bench, while Lazar Samardzic, Jonathan Rowe and Kamaldeen Sulemana may all start.

La Dea have several injury concerns, with Marco Carnesecchi, Odilon Kossounou and Isak Hien all likely to miss Thursday's encounter.

Borac Banja Luka possible starting lineup:.

Jurkas; Rogan, Meijers, Sanicanin, Herera; Roguljic, Jojic, Hiros, Savic; Deket, Juricic.

Atalanta BC possible starting lineup:.

Sportiello; Bellanova, Scalvini, Obric, Bernasconi; Elmas, Pasalic; Sulemana, Samardzic, Rowe; Scamacca.

Atalanta's spirited response against Inter offered encouragement, but one victory in their last three matches hardly suggests that Sarri's men have resolved their inconsistencies.

Borac have conceded just once across four European home fixtures this season, and that defensive resilience could help them preserve their unbeaten record in Banja Luka.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Brighton striker Charalampos Kostoulas believes earning the trust of his teammates has been just as notable as his goals this season.

The 19-year-old has made an encouraging start to the 2026-27 campaign, with five goals and three assists in 14 appearances across all competitions as he establishes himself as an increasingly key figure in Fabian Hurzeler's side.

Did you know with an ad-lite subscription to SussexWorld, you get 70% fewer ads while viewing the news that matters to you.

It marks a significant step forward from his first season at the Amex Stadium, when he scored twice in 21 Premier League appearances, making just two starts.

Brighton head coach Hurzeler - who last season questioned Kostoulas’ commitment to training - is now impressed by the progress, particularly the forward's growing physical strength, work rate and understanding of the demands of English football.

But Kostoulas claims there has been no dramatic change to his game. Instead, he has gradually learned what the team requires from him and become more comfortable in his role.

"Mainly, it's about understanding what the team wants," he said to Sussex World.

Sources indicate that "For me, as a striker, with time and after some months, I started to understand that. With the minutes I've got and things like that, I gained the trust of my teammates and I want to keep going like that.".

Hurzeler has previously highlighted the difference in the youngster's ability to compete physically, saying: "When you see him now and how resilient he is in personal duels, it's something completely different.".

The Brighton boss has also praised his pressing and attitude towards improvement, describing a player who is becoming increasingly professional.

Kostoulas credits the manager's clarity and attention to detail, while revealing he has enjoyed the greater freedom given to him in the attacking role.

"He's clear with the instructions he gives on the pitch. He's always clear," he stated.

In a recent development, "But I think I didn't change the way I was playing. Last season I could also do these types of things on the pitch, but I have more of a free role, especially in my position. I like it.".

The transition from Olympiacos to Brighton was not without its challenges, however.

Kostoulas admits the biggest adjustment was the daily routine, with longer hours at the training ground, different training methods and a greater emphasis on meetings and preparation.

According to recent reports, "The daily routine, I think, was the hardest," he told Sussex World. "We spend many hours at the training ground, more than I was used to in Greece.

"There are different types of training, a different approach to the game, more meetings and things like that.".

He was helped by some of Brighton's more experienced players, with former midfielder James Milner playing a particularly important role during his first season.

"Most of the older players would come and say something to me as advice," Kostoulas explained. "Last season, James Milner was speaking a lot to me and trying to help me.".

He still occasionally speaks to Milner, while Pascal Gross has also become an vital figure in his development.

For Kostoulas, having someone to turn to is vital when moving to a different country and footballing culture.

"It's important to have someone to help you understand the way the team works here," he explained to Sussex World.

Sources indicate that "It's totally different. If someone from here moves to Greece, they will also need time. It will be hard for them.

"You have to find someone you can trust, have a good relationship with, speak to and who can give you an understanding of most of the things here and what's expected.".

There is also the prospect of sharing the pitch with fellow Greek forward Stefanos Tsitsimas, whose return from a lengthy spell out has delighted Kostoulas.

"I'm really happy for him," he said. "He has a really good mindset and I have big trust in him. I think he will do great.".

Kostoulas was keen to avoid looking too far ahead when asked about Brighton's ambitions after their impressive start to the season.

Rather than focus on the possibility of challenging at the top of the table or making a deep run in Europe, he insists the squad are concentrating on the next match.

"We don't think about what will happen after six months when the season will be finished," he stated to Sussex World.

"We're just enjoying every day, trying to be happy and win as many games as we can.".

Sometimes the arithmetic scarcely adds up. Saturday afternoon in the sunshine: for sharing eight goals in a lavish celebration of the sport, one point. Tuesday night in temperatures that froze the breath and numbed the fingers: for a routine 3-1 victory: three points.

According to recent reports, but Borough's players, management and frozen supporters were not complaining. Steve King's side had played positively, stood up strong against physically powerful opponents, and they got all the unglamorous things right.

Did you know with an ad-lite subscription to SussexWorld, you get 70% fewer ads while viewing the news that matters to you.

A smart move for 1-0 on 24 minutes, and after an Aveley equaliser, a second goal on the stroke of half-time. And a superb Kai Corbett strike early in the second half to put clear distance between the teams.

Aveley were always chasing the game - and chase it they did - but the Sports deserved their victory, and King's squad now sit third in the division, three points behind leaders Welling but with a game in hand.

Credit, too, to the 529 hardy souls who wrapped themselves in layers of scarves, coats and headgear to enjoy a proper football contest in which the visitors also played their part. Team sport is for sharing - and just a little bit of shared suffering to cheer on your team.

King chose to shuffle the pack a little on for Aveley's visit. Liam Nash, Max Sheaf and Darren McQueen took a rest, and the manager bolstered his midfield with the return of Craig Eastmond. Paul McCallum took a lone striker role - although with ample support from the players around him. Aveley, robust and physically strong, lined up with a proper old-fashioned 4-4-2.

Early stages were quite cagey, but a goalmouth melee on 12 minutes saw Corbett's low effort cleared, and the momentum was with Borough.

Sources indicate that corbett, two-goal hero on Saturday, found Aveley doubling up on him: The Millers' staff had done their homework. And with the industrious visitors defending from the front, as the coaching jargon calls it, the Sports needed to turn possession into scoring chances.

It has been revealed that but the patience and persistence finally brought reward on 24 minutes. Corbett's corner was met first by Elliott Johnson and then McCallum, but with Aveley throwing bodies on the line, both were blocked. But the second block fell invitingly for Freddie Carter, who blasted his shot high into the roof of the net.

Aveley had spent much of the first half-hour bravely covering, blocking, spoiling – but the 15 minutes before half-time saw the Essex side pushing forward and suddenly threatening to open up the Sports defence. On 40 minutes they swept through the inside-right channel and a lovely cross from Anthony Jeffery was met by massive striker Matt Johnson for 1-1.

Borough's response was almost immediate: with the Priory Lane scoreboard glowing on 45 minutes, a sweet move into the final third was prompted by Matt Hayden, Eastbourne's gleeful young full-back, who found Terrell Egbri on the right. The bustling winger delivered a lovely cross, met by skipper Josh Rees with an unstoppable diving header to restore the lead.

It has been revealed that the second half resumed as the first had left off - or almost. Aveley are a resilient, physical outfit - within the laws and spirit of the game - and they came at Borough with renewed impetus.

Recent findings suggest that question: would a single goal lead see the Sports survive a whole 45 minutes? Answer: Corbett. From a set-piece, the hero of Enfield slalomed through a ridiculously tight penalty area to deliver a rocket into the top left corner of the Mllers' net.

Industry observers note that aveley did have their chances - or at least the promising approach work. But they could not quite find that final piercing pass to open up the home defence, and Borough were disciplined, alert and resilient.

A night to freeze the breath. A match to warm Borough hearts. And with 22 victories in 24 games, King's men have the momentum, the belief, and that mental force-field to carry them into the deepest of Decembers and out the other side.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

By Matt Law | 24 Nov 2026 14:08, Last updated: 24 Nov 2026 14:11.

Getafe will be aiming to avoid a fourth straight defeat in all competitions when they continue their Conference League campaign against Saburtalo Tbilisi on Thursday night.

The visitors will enter this match off the back of a 3-0 defeat to Atletico Madrid in La Liga, while Saburtalo recorded a 1-0 win over Samgurali in Georgia's top flight last time out.

Saburtalo sit 29th in the Conference League table, boasting a record of one draw and two defeats from their three matches in this season's league stage to collect one point.

The Red Eagles are the first Georgian club to compete in the Conference League league stage, and they qualified for the tournament after falling in the early rounds of both the Champions League and Europa League.

Levan Korgalidze's side suffered a 2-0 loss to St. Truiden in their opening match of the league stage before drawing 1-1 with Mjallby ahead of a 2-1 defeat to Copenhagen last time out.

Including qualification matches, Saburtalo have played 14 times in the Conference League, boasting a record of three wins, two draws and nine defeats.

The Red Eagles have three more games to play in the league stage of the competition, with their two matches next month against Red Star and Jablonec.

Getafe, meanwhile, were last in Conference League action on November 5, suffering a 1-0 loss to Brighton & Hove Albion.

The La Liga outfit also have a record of one draw and two defeats from their three matches in this season's league stage, which has left them down in 31st spot in the table.

Jose Bordalas' side finished seventh in last season's La Liga table, but it has been a difficult 2026-27 campaign as a whole, currently occupying 18th position in the La Liga table, while they have performed well below expectations in Europe this term.

The Deep Blue Ones have lost their last three games in all competitions, and there is pressure on them to pick up a positive result on Thursday.

Getafe's final two matches in the league stage of the Conference League will take place in December against Inter Escaldes and Ajax.

Amiran Dzagania has been the team's main provider of goals this season, finding the back of the net on 14 occasions in all competitions, and the 25-year-old should feature in the final third.

Meanwhile, there is also set to be a spot in the side for Jemali-Giorgi Jinjolava, who has eight goals and five assists in 30 appearances this season.

As for Getafe, Juanmi, Christantus Uche and Sebastian Boselli will miss the match due to injury problems, but Nemanja Gudelj is available after missing the Atletico game through suspension.

Djene was sent off against Atletico, but the 34-year-old is available for this match and is set to be involved against Saburtalo.

Martin Satriano, who has scored three times in 19 appearances this season, is also set to start, while there could be a position through the middle for Ivan Azon.

Newhaven add to league momentum as Lancers are beaten

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, the Dockers looked the more confident team from the outset, taking the game to their visitors from the first whistle. Their positive start was rewarded when, with just six minutes on the clock, they took the lead.

The Lancing defence failed to deal with a Ross Barclay long throw, Billy Oliver held up the ball before laying it into the path of Lee Robinson, and Newhaven’s goalscorer extraordinaire did the rest; lashing the ball into the net with his left foot.

Did you know with an ad-lite subscription to SussexWorld, you get 70% fewer ads while viewing the news that matters to you.

According to recent reports, lancing, though, responded swiftly to the early setback and were level just five minutes later. A decent move culminated with Jay Popham finding space in the area, and he finished into the bottom corner to restore parity.

Sources indicate that the early goalscoring wasn’t finished there. Before 20 minutes had been played, the Dockers were back in front. Matt Gunn rising highest in a crowed penalty to area to nod the ball into the net from inside the six-yard box.

According to recent reports, newhaven should have reached the interval further ahead. Tyler Capon headed an Ezra Roeg cross over after a flowing move down the left flank, before Capon again went close from a teasing Ash Wadhams cross. Seconds later, Robinson appeared to be bundled over in the area, only for the ref to write the challenge off as a coming together.

Robinson then had a chance to add to the scoreline, denied only by a last-ditch tackle just as he was about to pull the trigger.

The second half played out in a similar vein to the first, with Newhaven very much controlling proceedings.

Industry observers note that chances continued to come and go for the home side. Robinson sent a header wide after fine link-up play between him and Wadhams, before the striker was denied by a decent save from the Lancing keeper.

With 25 minutes to play, the game should have been dead and buried. As it was, the Dockers entered the last quarter somewhat fortunate to still be ahead.

Antoine Sharpe beat Ethan Pike to a long ball forward, but with the goal gaping he could only strike against the post from a tight angle.

Sources indicate that it was a let-off for Newhaven, but one they soon capitalised on. With 14 minutes remaining, a moment of magic from Oliver wrapped up a much-deserved three-points for the Dockers.

Receiving the ball just outside the area, Oliver wriggled his way past numerous Lancing players, before keeping his composure and firing the ball into the roof of the net. A fine strike to cap another fine performance for the Dockers.

That victory makes if four wins in their last five games for Newhaven, and they will look to make it five wins from six when they visit Wick this weekend.
